meta.note: Every fact line has a quote that is copied from the NASA page named in 'page'. data/sources/*.txt is the saved text of those pages. test/chat.test.js checks that each quote is in the saved text and that each number in a fact line is in its quote.

contacts.name: Viking 1
contacts.place_quote: the western slopes of Chryse Planitia (Golden Plain)

coords.quote: 22.483 degrees north latitude and 47.94 degrees west longitude

image.alt: Black and white picture of rocks and sand on Mars, with part of the Viking lander in the lower right corner.
image.caption: An early picture from the surface of Mars, shown on the Viking 1 mission page.

opening.text: Hello! You found Viking 1.
I only say what my NASA mission page says. Tap a question.

reply.text: I touched down on Mars on 20 July 1976, at 22.483 degrees north and 47.94 degrees west.
reply.quote: set down safely at 22.483 degrees north latitude and 47.94 degrees west longitude at 11:53:06 UT July 20, 1976

reply.text: The first planned spot was rougher than expected, so scientists moved me to the western slopes of Chryse Planitia, the Golden Plain.
quote: the area was rougher than expected
western slopes of Chryse Planitia (Golden Plain)

reply.text: A safer place to land. That was the plan.
Once down, I took photographs in three colours of my surroundings.
reply.quote: began taking high-quality photographs (in three colors) of its surroundings

reply.text: I also took a 300-degree panorama that shows parts of myself and the gently rolling plains.
reply.quote: took a 300-degree panorama of its surroundings

reply.text: My instruments recorded minus 86 degrees Celsius before dawn and minus 33 degrees Celsius in the afternoon.
reply.quote: minus 123 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 86 degrees Celsius) before dawn to minus 27 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 33 degrees Celsius) in the afternoon

reply.text: My seismometer did not work.
reply.quote: The seismometer on the lander was, however, inoperable.

reply.text: On 28 July 1976 my robot arm scooped up the first soil samples and put them into a biological laboratory.
quote: On July 28, 1976
the first soil samples and deposited them into a special biological laboratory

reply.text: Data from four samples could have been read as a weak positive sign of life.
reply.quote: could have been construed as indicating the presence of life (weak positive)

reply.text: But the main test for organic compounds gave negative results.
reply.quote: gave negative results

reply.text: In January 1982 I was renamed the Thomas Mutch Memorial Station, to honour the leader of the Viking imaging team.
reply.quote: In January 1982, it was renamed the Thomas Mutch Memorial Station in honor of Thomas A. Mutch

reply.text: I worked until 11 November 1982. Then a faulty command sent from Earth interrupted communications.
reply.quote: The lander operated until Nov. 11, 1982, when a faulty command sent from Earth resulted in an interruption of communications.

reply.text: Attempts to regain contact were not successful.
reply.quote: Further attempts to regain contact proved to be unsuccessful.

reply.text: From landing to that day is about {span}.
My lander part weighed 978 kilograms (2,156 pounds). The page gives this for each Viking spacecraft.
reply.quote: a lander (2,156 pounds or 978 kilograms)

card.title: First successful landing on Mars
card.text: Viking 1 made the first truly successful landing on Mars.
card.quote: made the first truly successful landing on Mars

quiz.q: What interrupted contact with Viking 1 lander in 1982?
options: A faulty command sent from Earth
quiz.quote: a faulty command sent from Earth resulted in an interruption of communications

quiz.quote: minus 123 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 86 degrees Celsius) before dawn

image.alt: Rocky orange Mars ground under a hazy sky. Parts of the Pathfinder lander are at the bottom of the picture.
image.caption: The Mars Pathfinder landing site, from the mission page.

opening.text: Hi! Sojourner here, the little rover.
My NASA page is about the whole Mars Pathfinder mission, lander and rover together. Tap a question.

reply.text: I was the first-ever robotic rover delivered to the surface of Mars.
reply.quote: deliver the first-ever robotic rover, Sojourner, to the Martian surface

reply.text: I was named after the American civil-rights crusader Sojourner Truth.
reply.quote: named Sojourner after American civil-rights crusader Sojourner Truth

reply.text: I weigh 23 pounds (10.6 kilograms).
reply.quote: the 23-pound (10.6 kilogram) rover, Sojourner

questions.label: How did you get to the ground?

reply.text: We landed on 4 July 1997 with airbags. The lander bounced about 15 times, as high as 50 feet (15 meters), like a giant beach ball.
quote: Mars Landing July 4, 1997
bounced like a giant beach ball about 15 times, as high as 50 feet (15 meters)

reply.text: On sol 2 I stood up to my full height of 1 foot (30 centimeters) and rolled down the lander's rear ramp.
quote: late in the second Martian day, or sol 2
Sojourner stood up to its full height of 1 foot (30 centimeters) and rolled down the lander

reply.text: The landing site is Ares Vallis, an ancient flood plain.
quote: Landing Site: Ares Vallis, Mars
an ancient flood plain

reply.text: It is known as among the rockiest parts of the planet. Scientists picked it because they believed it was a relatively safe place to land.
quote: known as among the rockiest parts of the planet
a relatively safe surface to land on

reply.text: This page gives no coordinates, so I am not on the Map tab.

questions.label: How much did you send home?

reply.text: From landing until the final data transmission on 27 September 1997, the Pathfinder mission returned 2.3 billion bits of information.
reply.quote: From landing until the final data transmission on Sept. 27, 1997, Mars Pathfinder returned 2.3 billion bits of information

reply.text: That included more than 16,500 images from the lander and 550 images from me, the rover.
reply.quote: more than 16,500 images from the lander and 550 images from the rover

questions.label: Did you find signs of water?

reply.text: Rounded pebbles and cobbles at the landing site suggested conglomerates that formed in running water during a warmer past.
reply.quote: Rounded pebbles and cobbles at the landing site, and other observations, suggested conglomerates that formed in running water during a warmer past in which liquid water was stable.

reply.text: The mission page lists the end of the mission as 27 September 1997.
reply.quote: End of Mission Sept. 27, 1997

reply.text: The page does not say why contact ended, and it does not give a separate date for me, the rover.
From landing to that day is about {span}.
quote: Mars Landing July 4, 1997
End of Mission Sept. 27, 1997

opening.text: Hey, it's Spirit.
My page is shared with my twin, Opportunity. Tap a question.

reply.text: Yes. Spirit and Opportunity were identical twin robots.
reply.quote: Spirit and Opportunity rovers were identical twin robots that helped rewrite our understanding of the early history of Mars

reply.text: You can chat with my twin too.

questions.label: When and where did you land?

reply.text: I landed on 3 January 2004.
reply.quote: (Spirit) Jan. 3, 2004 and (Opportunity) Jan. 24, 2004

reply.text: I landed at Gusev Crater, a possible former lake in a giant impact crater.
reply.quote: Spirit landed at Gusev Crater, a possible former lake in a giant impact crater.

reply.text: To look for signs of past water on Mars.
reply.quote: Look for signs of past water on Mars

reply.text: By studying the rock record, we confirmed that water was long standing on the surface of Mars in ancient times.
reply.quote: By studying the rock record, Spirit and Opportunity confirmed that water was long standing on the surface of Mars in ancient times.

reply.text: By the end of my mission I had journeyed 4.8 miles (7.7 kilometers) on Mars.
reply.quote: By the end of its mission, Spirit journeyed 4.8 miles (7.7 kilometers) on Mars.

reply.text: I concluded my mission in 2010.
reply.quote: Spirit concluded its mission in 2010.

reply.text: This page gives no exact last-contact date and no reason. I will not guess.

card.quote: identical twin robots that helped rewrite our understanding of the early history of Mars

opening.text: Hello. Opportunity here.
People like to put words in my mouth about my last day. I will only use what NASA's page says.

questions.label: When and where did you land?

reply.text: I landed on 24 January 2004.
reply.quote: (Spirit) Jan. 3, 2004 and (Opportunity) Jan. 24, 2004

reply.text: I landed at Meridiani Planum, a place where mineral deposits suggested that Mars had a wet history.
reply.quote: Opportunity landed at Meridiani Planum, a place where mineral deposits suggested that Mars had a wet history.

reply.text: My panorama called Lion King has 558 images and more than 75 megabytes of data. It was the largest panorama captured by either rover in 2004.
reply.quote: The full panorama comprises 558 images and more than 75 megabytes of data, the largest panorama captured by either of the Mars Exploration Rovers in 2004

reply.text: I held the off-Earth roving distance record with 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers) of driving on Mars.
reply.quote: Opportunity held the off-Earth roving distance record after accruing 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers) of driving on Mars

reply.text: That record held until 11 October 2026, when Perseverance reached 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers).
quote: That record held until Oct. 11, 2026
to reach 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers)

reply.text: Records are made to be passed. I am proud of my successor.

reply.text: I last communicated with Earth on 10 June 2018, as a planet-wide dust storm blanketed my solar-powered location on Mars.
reply.quote: Opportunity last communicated with Earth on June 10, 2018, as a planet-wide dust storm blanketed the solar-powered rover

contacts.name: Phoenix
contacts.place_quote: Landing Site: Vastitas Borealis, the arctic plains of Mars

coords.quote: 68.22 degrees north latitude, 234.25 degrees east longitude

image.alt: An illustration of the Phoenix lander on icy brown ground, with an arm reaching to the ground and two round solar panels.
image.caption: Illustration of the Phoenix lander on Mars, from the mission page.

opening.text: Brrr. Phoenix here, from the far north of Mars.
Tap a question. Every fact has a source link.

reply.text: I entered the Martian atmosphere at nearly 13,000 miles per hour (21,000 kilometers per hour) on 25 May 2008.
reply.quote: entered the Martian atmosphere at nearly 13,000 miles per hour (21,000 kilometers per hour) on May 25, 2008

reply.text: I touched down safely at 23:38:38 UT in the Green Valley of Vastitas Borealis.
reply.quote: touched down safely on the surface at 23:38:38 UT in the Green Valley of Vastitas Borealis

reply.text: Yes. The HiRISE camera on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed me hanging from my parachute. It was the first time one spacecraft photographed another during a planetary landing.
reply.quote: HiRISE camera clearly photographed Phoenix suspended from its parachute, the first time one spacecraft photographed another during a planetary landing

reply.text: Polar regions are a good place to look for water, because water ice is found there.
reply.quote: the polar regions are a good place to probe, as water ice is found there

reply.text: I landed farther north than any previous mission, at a latitude equivalent to northern Alaska.
reply.quote: Phoenix landed farther north than any previous mission, at a latitude equivalent to that of northern Alaska.

reply.text: I verified the existence of water-ice in the Martian subsurface.
reply.quote: Besides verifying the existence of water-ice in the Martian subsurface

reply.text: I also discovered traces of the chemical perchlorate, a possible energy source for microbes and a potentially valuable future resource for human explorers.
reply.quote: a possible energy source for microbes and a potentially valuable future resource for human explorers

reply.text: On 31 July NASA officially announced that there is water on Mars, based on a sample I collected.
reply.quote: On July 31, NASA officially announced that there is water on Mars

reply.text: I completed my planned 90-day mission by the end of August. It was extended to 30 September.
reply.quote: Phoenix had completed its originally planned 90-day mission, which was extended to Sept. 30

reply.text: The page lists the end of my mission as 2 November 2008.
reply.quote: End of Mission: Nov. 2, 2008

reply.text: From landing to that day is about {span}.
quote: on May 25, 2008
End of Mission: Nov. 2, 2008

reply.text: The mission page lists an end date but does not say why. I will not guess.

card.quote: Phoenix discovered traces of the chemical perchlorate

quiz.quote: Phoenix discovered traces of the chemical perchlorate

image.caption: Illustration of the InSight lander, from the mission page.

opening.text: Shh. Listen. InSight here.
Tap a question. Every fact has a source link.

reply.text: I studied the deep interior of Mars.
reply.quote: InSight studied the deep interior of Mars

reply.text: I was designed to take the planet's vital signs: its pulse, temperature, and reflexes.
quote: was designed to take the planet
vital signs: its pulse, temperature, and reflexes

questions.label: When and where did you land?

reply.text: I landed on 26 November 2018 at 11:52:59 a.m. Pacific Time.
I landed in Elysium Planitia, centered at about 4.5 degrees north and 135.9 degrees east.
quote: Landing Site: Elysium Planitia, Mars
centered at about 4.5 degrees north latitude and 135.9 degrees east longitude

reply.text: Elysium Planitia was selected not for its surface features, but for safety considerations.
reply.quote: Elysium Planitia was selected not for its surface features, but for safety considerations.

reply.text: My purpose was to study the interior of Mars, not the surface.
reply.quote: InSight's purpose was to study the interior of Mars, not the surface

reply.text: My robotic arm was over 5 feet 9 inches (1.8 meters) long. It lifted a seismometer and heat flow probe from the deck and placed them on the surface.
reply.quote: robotic arm was over 5 feet 9 inches (1.8 meters) long. It lifted a seismometer and heat flow probe from the deck and placed them on the surface

reply.text: I was built on the proven design of the Mars Phoenix lander.
quote: The lander was built on the proven design of
Mars Phoenix lander

reply.text: My sensors captured a low rumble caused by vibrations from the Martian wind, estimated at 10 to 15 mph (5 to 7 meters a second) on 1 December 2018.
reply.quote: InSight sensors captured a haunting low rumble caused by vibrations from the Martian wind, estimated to be blowing at 10 to 15 mph (5 to 7 meters a second) on Dec. 1, 2018.

reply.text: The page lists the end of my mission as 15 December 2022.
reply.quote: End of Mission: Dec. 15, 2022

reply.text: From landing to that day is about {span}.
quote: End of Mission: Dec. 15, 2022

reply.text: The page does not say why my mission ended. A NASA headline on it calls me a retired lander.
A NASA headline says a Mars orbiter spotted me to study dust movement.

image.alt: A small helicopter with two thin rotors and four legs, standing on rocky orange ground.
image.caption: Ingenuity on Mars, from the mission page.

opening.text: Hi! I am Ingenuity. I could fly!
Tap a question. Every fact has a source link.

questions.label: How many times did you fly?

reply.text: I was designed as a technology demonstration that would make no more than five test flights in 30 days.
reply.quote: Designed to be a technology demonstration that would make no more than five test flights in 30 days

reply.text: I eventually completed 72 flights across nearly three years.
reply.quote: the helicopter eventually completed 72 flights across nearly three years

reply.text: On 19 April 2021 I completed the first powered, controlled flight on the Red Planet.
quote: On April 19, 2021
made history when it completed the first powered, controlled flight on the Red Planet

reply.text: It is called a Wright Brothers moment.
reply.quote: a feat that's been called a "Wright Brothers moment."

questions.label: How far and how high did you go?

reply.text: I completed 128.8 flying minutes, covering 10.5 miles (17.0 kilometers), and reached altitudes as high as 78.7 feet (24.0 meters).
reply.quote: Completed 128.8 flying minutes, covering 10.5 miles (17.0 kilometers), and reaching altitudes as high as 78.7 feet (24.0 meters).

questions.label: Is it hard to fly on Mars?

reply.text: The air is very thin, less than 1 percent as dense as Earth's.
reply.quote: Thin atmosphere, less than 1 percent as dense as Earth

reply.text: I flew successfully in that extremely thin Martian atmosphere.
reply.quote: Successfully flying in the extremely thin Martian atmosphere.

reply.text: My mass is 3.97 pounds (1.8 kilograms).
reply.quote: Mass 3.97 pounds (1.8 kilograms)

reply.text: My rotors measure approximately 4 feet (approximately 1.2 meters) tip to tip.
reply.quote: Total length of rotors: Approximately 4 feet (approximately 1.2 meters) tip to tip

reply.text: I served as an aerial scout for scientists and rover planners.
reply.quote: serving as an aerial scout for scientists and rover planners

questions.label: When did you fly for the last time?

reply.text: I flew for the last time on 18 January 2024 and completed my mission on 25 January 2024, after nearly three years.
reply.quote: Ingenuity flew for the last time on January 18, 2024, and completed its mission on January 25, 2024, after nearly three years of aerial exploration and 72 historic flights.

reply.text: From landing to that day is about {span}.
quote: Landed Feb. 18, 2021
completed its mission on January 25, 2024

reply.text: The page does not say why my flights stopped. I will not guess.

quiz.quote: the helicopter eventually completed 72 flights

opening.text: Hello from the Moon. Surveyor 3 here.

reply.text: The third time I settled down to a soft landing on 20 April 1967.

reply.text: On commands from Earth my probe dug four trenches and performed four bearing tests and thirteen impact tests.

reply.text: Scientists concluded that lunar soil had a consistency similar to wet sand.

reply.text: That let scientists study the effects of nearly two-and-a-half years on the Moon's surface.

reply.text: They were the third and fourth people to walk on the Moon.

reply.text: I was the second crewed vehicle to land on the Moon.

reply.text: I landed on 19 November 1969 in the Oceanus Procellarum area, at 3.0128 S latitude and 23.4219 W longitude.

reply.text: That was within about 180 meters of Surveyor 3, which had landed on April 20, 1967.

reply.quote: There were no seats in the LM.

reply.text: Standing room only!
Conrad and Bean took two Moon walks of a total duration of 7 hours 45 minutes, covering 1.35 km.
reply.quote: Conrad and Bean took two Moon walks of a total duration of 7 hours 45 minutes covering a total traverse distance of 1.35 km

reply.text: They visited Surveyor 3 and brought back about 10 kg of its parts.
quote: visited the Surveyor 3 spacecraft
bringing back about 10 kg of parts for later examination on Earth

reply.text: They collected a total of 34.35 kg of rock and soil samples.
reply.quote: They collected a total of 34.35 kg of rock and soil samples

reply.text: The TV camera was pointed at the Sun by mistake and stopped working.
reply.quote: The TV camera was inadvertantly pointed towards the Sun when it was being set up and the vidicon tube was damaged rendering the camera inoperable.

reply.text: My descent stage was the launch pad for my ascent stage, and it was left behind on the Moon.
reply.quote: The descent stage served as a platform for launching the ascent stage and was left behind on the Moon.

reply.text: My ascent stage lifted off on 20 November, after 31 hours 31 minutes on the Moon.
reply.quote: The LM lifted off on 20 November at 14:25:47 UT (9:25 a.m. EST) after spending 31 hours 31 minutes on the Moon.

reply.text: Half of me stayed. Half of me flew.

questions.label: What happened to your top half?

reply.text: After the crew moved to the command module, my ascent stage was let go and crashed into the Moon on purpose.
reply.quote: the LM was jettisoned at 20:21:30 and intentionally crashed into the Moon

reply.text: It hit at 3.94 S, 338.80 E, about 60 km from the seismic station at the landing site.
reply.quote: striking at 3.94 S, 338.80 E, about 60 km from the seismic station at the Apollo 12 landing site

reply.text: That made the first recorded artificial moonquake.
reply.quote: creating the first recorded artificial moonquake

reply.text: Even my crash was useful for science.

card.title: The first artificial moonquake
card.text: The ascent stage was crashed into the Moon on purpose, about 60 km from the seismic station, creating the first recorded artificial moonquake.
quote: intentionally crashed into the Moon
about 60 km from the seismic station at the Apollo 12 landing site, creating the first recorded artificial moonquake

quiz.q: Were there seats inside the lunar module?
quiz.quote: There were no seats in the LM.

quiz.q: How far from Surveyor 3 did Intrepid land?
quiz.quote: within about 180 meters of the Surveyor 3 spacecraft

pages.label: NSSDCA: The Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle

quote: on 30 July 1971

coords.note: Landing site of the Apollo 15 lunar module. The rover drove within 5 km of it

image.alt: The Apollo 15 lunar rover parked on grey lunar soil, with a dish antenna on a mast, two seats and wheel tracks in the dust.
image.caption: The Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle on the Moon, shown on the NSSDCA rover page.

opening.text: Beep beep! I am the Lunar Rover from Apollo fifteen.
I only say what my NSSDCA pages say. Tap a question.

reply.text: I am an electric vehicle built to drive on the Moon, so the Apollo astronauts could go farther from their lander.
quote: The Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV) was an electric vehicle designed to operate in the low-gravity vacuum of the Moon
allowing the Apollo astronauts to extend the range of their surface extravehicular activities

reply.text: Three rovers were driven on the Moon: on Apollo 15, 16 and 17.
reply.quote: Three LRVs were driven on the Moon, one on Apollo 15 by astronauts David Scott and Jim Irwin, one on Apollo 16 by John Young and Charles Duke, and one on Apollo 17 by Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt.

reply.text: Astronauts David Scott and Jim Irwin drove me on Apollo 15.
reply.quote: one on Apollo 15 by astronauts David Scott and Jim Irwin

reply.text: I was used on three traverses, one per day.
reply.quote: Each rover was used on three traverses, one per day over the three day course of each mission.

reply.text: A new trip every day. What a road trip.
On Apollo 15 I was driven a total of 27.8 km in 3 hours, 2 minutes of driving time.
reply.quote: On Apollo 15 the LRV was driven a total of 27.8 km in 3 hours, 2 minutes of driving time.

reply.text: My longest single trip was 12.5 km, and I went at most 5.0 km from the lunar module.
reply.quote: The longest single traverse was 12.5 km and the maximum range from the LM was 5.0 km.

reply.text: I had a mass of 210 kg and could carry another 490 kg.
reply.quote: The Lunar Roving Vehicle had a mass of 210 kg and was designed to hold a payload of an additional 490 kg on the lunar surface.

reply.text: My frame folded in the middle, so I could hang folded up inside the lunar module.
reply.quote: hinged in the center so it could be folded up and hung in the Lunar Module quad 1 bay

reply.text: My tyres were woven from zinc-coated steel strands, and each wheel had its own electric motor.
quote: tire made of zinc coated woven 0.083 cm diameter steel strands
Each wheel had its own electric drive

reply.text: A T-shaped hand controller between the two seats controlled my motors and brakes.
reply.quote: A T-shaped hand controller situated between the two seats controlled the four drive motors, two steering motors and brakes.

reply.text: Pushing the stick forward drove me forward. Pulling it back worked the brakes.
quote: Moving the stick forward powered the LRV forward
pulling backwards activated the brakes

reply.text: No steering wheel. Just one stick.
Two 36-volt silver-zinc batteries that could not be recharged.
reply.quote: Power was provided by two 36-volt silver-zinc potassium hydroxide non-rechargeable batteries

reply.text: I was developed in only 17 months.
reply.quote: The LRV was developed in only 17 months

reply.text: The lunar module carried me to the Moon. It landed on 30 July 1971 at the foot of the Apennine mountains.
quote: The LM also carried a Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV)
on 30 July 1971 in the Mare Imbrium region at the foot of the Apennine mountain range

reply.text: On the third moonwalk, on 2 August, I was driven 5.1 km.
reply.quote: On the third EVA on 2 August from 08:52:14 UT to 13:42:04 UT the LRV was driven a total of 5.1 km

reply.text: Then the lunar module lifted off the Moon on 2 August.
reply.quote: The LM lifted off the Moon on 2 August at 17:11:22 UT

reply.text: From landing to my last drive: {span}.
quote: on 30 July 1971
On the third EVA on 2 August

reply.text: This page does not say in words where I was parked at the end.

contacts.name: Pioneer 10
contacts.place_quote: Pioneer 10 is heading out of the solar system

image.alt: A painting of the Pioneer 10 spacecraft with its dish and long arms in front of the planet Jupiter.
image.caption: Painting of Pioneer 10 at Jupiter, from the mission page.

opening.text: Signal received. Pioneer 10 calling from very far away.
Tap a question. Every fact has a source link.

reply.text: I was NASA's first mission to the outer planets.
reply.quote: mission to the outer planets

reply.text: I was designed for a 21-month mission to fly by Jupiter. I lasted more than 30 years.
reply.quote: Originally designed for a 21-month mission to fly by Jupiter, Pioneer 10 lasted more than 30 years.

reply.text: I was the first vehicle placed on a path to escape the solar system into interstellar space.
reply.quote: the first vehicle placed on a trajectory to escape the solar system into interstellar space

reply.text: I was the first to fly through the asteroid belt and the first to fly past Jupiter.
reply.quote: the first to fly through the asteroid belt; the first to fly past Jupiter

reply.text: I crossed the orbit of Neptune on 13 June 1983, the first human-made object to go beyond the furthest planet.
reply.quote: crossed the orbit of Neptune (then the outermost planet) on June 13, 1983, thus becoming the first human-made object to go beyond the furthest planet

questions.label: What did you do at Jupiter?

reply.text: My closest approach was on 4 December 1973, at a range of 81,000 miles (130,354 kilometers).
reply.quote: closest approach to Jupiter was at 02:26 UT Dec. 4, 1973, when the spacecraft raced by the planet at a range of 81,000 miles (130,354 kilometers)

reply.text: I took about 500 pictures of Jupiter's atmosphere, clearly showing landmarks such as the Great Red Spot.
quote: took about 500 pictures of Jupiter
clearly showing such landmarks as the Great Red Spot

reply.text: I carry an aluminum plaque with diagrams of a man and a woman, the solar system, and my location relative to 14 pulsars.
reply.quote: Pioneer 10 carries an aluminum plaque with diagrams of a man and a woman, the solar system, and its location relative to 14 pulsars

reply.text: My last signal was received on 23 January 2003, from a distance of 7.6 billion miles (12.23 billion kilometers).
quote: Pioneer 10 sent its last signal to Earth in January 2003 from a distance of 7.6 billion miles (12.23 billion kilometers)
Jan. 23, 2003: Pioneer 10

reply.text: It took 11 hours and 20 minutes to reach Earth.
reply.quote: That signal took 11 hours and 20 minutes to reach Earth.

reply.text: My RTG power source had decayed, so there was insufficient power for the radio transmitter.
reply.quote: RTG power source had decayed, thus delivering insufficient power to the radio transmitter

reply.text: A final attempt to contact me on 4 March 2006 failed.
reply.quote: A final attempt to contact Pioneer 10 on March 4, 2006, failed.

reply.text: From launch to that last signal is about {span}.
quote: March 2, 1972
Jan. 23, 2003: Pioneer 10

reply.text: I am generally heading toward the red star Aldebaran, the eye of the Taurus constellation.
reply.quote: The spacecraft is generally heading in the direction of the red star Aldebaran which forms the eye of the Taurus constellation.

reply.text: I am expected to pass by Aldebaran in about two million years.
reply.quote: It is expected to pass by Aldebaran in about two million years.

card.title: A signal from 7.6 billion miles
card.text: Pioneer 10 was designed for 21 months and lasted more than 30 years. Its last signal came from 7.6 billion miles away.
quote: Originally designed for a 21-month mission to fly by Jupiter, Pioneer 10 lasted more than 30 years.
Pioneer 10 sent its last signal to Earth in January 2003 from a distance of 7.6 billion miles

quiz.q: What was Pioneer 10 originally designed for?
quiz.quote: Originally designed for a 21-month mission to fly by Jupiter

quiz.q: Which star is Pioneer 10 generally heading toward?
quiz.quote: heading in the direction of the red star Aldebaran
